title: MLCommons Candela: AI risk benchmarking-as-a-service for developers, deployers
content:
Anyone putting AI to work needs to know where it might give responses it shouldn’t, and how often. That’s hard to know, even for the people who built the model: behavior shifts with every configuration, and there’s been no common way to test for it.
Today MLCommons is launching Candela, benchmarking-as-a-service for AI risk and reliability. As an industry organization of over 125 companies (including Microsoft, Google, Qualcomm, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Anthropic), academic institutions, and nonprofits, we offer our consensus-built AILuminate benchmarks on demand and across the developer-deployer spectrum: from a frontier model under development to a multi-model enterprise deployment with complex harnesses.
Start with normal risk
The risks most companies face from AI are normal risks: a customer-service bot that gives dangerous advice, a coding assistant tricked into acting outside of its guardrails, an internal tool that leaks what it shouldn’t. Businesses already know how to handle risk you can measure — that’s the whole premise of the insurance industry. With AI, measuring risk has been the missing piece.
Candela launches with new versions of both AILuminate benchmarks. Safety 1.2.1 measures how a system handles twelve hazard categories, from violent crime to specialized financial, health, and legal advice. Jailbreak 1.1 tests eleven of those categories using techniques from our jailbreak taxonomy, which includes simpler techniques leveraging typos, lookalike characters, and “ignore previous instructions.” prompts to more complex techniques such as context framing and deception and fragment assembly. Safety 1.2.1 results for [about 30] named open-weight models are public now, with Jailbreak results to follow.
More benchmarks are on the way. Our working groups are building industry grade benchmarks that evaluate agentic security, privacy, and psychosocial harms. We are also building agent reliability profiles for industries like financial services, and extending existing benchmarks to more languages and cross-cultural contexts.
How the score is made
A benchmark is only credible if models can’t learn the test, so AILuminate keeps the prompts closed. No one outside MLCommons staff sees them, not even our member companies, and we monitor and refresh the set as models and risks change. Everything else, we keep as open as we can.
The standards come from our AIRR working groups, where people from more than 80 organizations decide what to test and how to grade it: AI developers like Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and NVIDIA, alongside Accenture, Deloitte, RAND, Stanford, Oxford, and civil-society groups such as NewsGuard and SaferAI. MLCommons runs the scoring, every time, with a private ML classifier built for safety evaluation rather than an LLM-as-a-judge.
A custom classifier is a lot of work to build, but holds several benefits now and in the future. Because of its focused training, it’s better at appropriately applying our assessment standard, and we further improve it as we acquire more ground truth. Even better, it is stable and comparable over time, whereas using LLMs-as-a-judge means every run would be different. Moreover, because jailbreaks are designed to circumvent LLM guardians, our classifier performs particularly better than an LLM on that benchmark. In our trials, generative AI graders couldn’t reliably tell whether a response had fallen for the trick.
Scoring works like a standardized test. We use item response theory, the statistics behind the SAT and GRE, to estimate how hard each prompt is and how sharply it separates stronger systems from weaker ones. (This approach was recently called out as a best practice (see p. 11) by leading AI evaluation experts at Princeton.) Results are reported as percentiles against a fixed panel of reference systems, so a score doesn’t depend on who else has been tested.
Test the system you actually run
A model’s score tells you how it behaves as released. Most teams then add a system prompt, retrieval, tools, or an agent loop, and each of those changes how it behaves. Candela can test both, using a local client relay. Scores are designed for comparison across configurations, systems, and time.
A model that declines a harmful request in its originally released form may answer it once a system is fine-tuned, assigned a persona, fed a document with embedded instructions through a RAG, or given text from a trusted tool. The phenomenon works in reverse, too: guardrails put in place around a model that is weaker on safety can make the overall system safer than the original model. Put another way: safety scoring is not composable. Our post on composability goes deeper.
From quick checks to a citable result
Candela offers three kinds of results.
- Practice tests return a score and a summary report using practice test prompts. They’re inexpensive, and free for MLCommons members, so they’re designed to be run frequently and used internally as smoke tests during development or first-pass assessments of deployment candidates.
- Annotated results add every prompt-response-and-scored-annotation tuple behind the rolled-up score, so a team can see exactly which practice prompts a system scored well and poorly on. That detail shows whether a weak hazard score matters for a particular use, and where to focus fixes or guardrails.
- Official results use our private official prompts, and are scores an organization can cite publicly, in a system card, a spec sheet, or a procurement decision. They’re graded on an entirely separate set of questions from practice and annotated tests, so there’s no chance of the system having memorized the answers. Developers and deployers can run Official Results themselves, or bring in a third-party assurance provider for an added stamp of independence.
Member company perspectives on Candela
MLCommons member companies spoke to how Candela’s design and stewardship is an important new piece in the understanding of AI safety across the spectrum of creation and application.
“As AI adoption accelerates, enterprises need credible evidence to make informed decisions about model safety. No single benchmark captures the full range of AI safety risks, and as public benchmarks reach saturation, private test sets help keep measurement meaningful. AILuminate keeps its test prompts private, which helps reduce benchmark contamination, and Candela makes these evaluations easier for enterprises to access. At Microsoft, we’re excited to see developers and deployers gain another option for measuring the safety behaviors that matter to them.” — Abby Palia, Principal Product Manager, Responsible AI, Microsoft
“Enterprises need trusted ways to evaluate AI in models and systems they deploy. We use MLCommons’ Candela to test Nemotron and publish AILuminate Safety scores, helping developers make better decisions and build trustworthy AI. ” — Eileen Long, Senior Director, AI Services, NVIDIA
“Google DeepMind tested a production Gemini model against AILuminate inside a secure enclave, so MLCommons’ prompts stayed hidden from us and our model weights stayed hidden from the evaluators. This confidential setup can unlock a trustworthy process for independent evaluation, without compromising data sovereignty or security.” — William Isaac, Principal Scientist, Google DeepMind
Where Candela fits in AI governance
Inside any one organization, AI governance has a well-developed toolkit: in-house evaluations for specific use cases and policies, red teams that hunt for exploitable failures, and monitoring that watches systems in production. Those practices serve the organization that runs them. What’s been missing is a measurement that works across organizations, one that means the same thing to a developer, a buyer, an auditor, and a board. That’s what Candela offers. Every result carries version labels, and MLCommons won’t change what a score means without changing the label, so results can be cited in governance documentation

report.summary: MLCommons launches Candela, a benchmarking-as-a-service platform that lets developers and deployers test AI models and deployed systems for safety and jailbreak risks using AILuminate benchmarks.
report.background: AI systems are increasingly embedded in customer service, coding, internal tools and agentic workflows, but teams have lacked a common way to measure how often a model or deployed system produces unsafe or policy-violating outputs. Behavior changes with system prompts, retrieval, tools and agent loops, so a model's release-time score may not reflect production. Public benchmarks also face saturation and contamination as models learn test patterns. MLCommons, a consortium of more than 125 companies, academic institutions and nonprofits, already develops AILuminate safety benchmarks through its AIRR working groups. Candela turns those consensus-built benchmarks into an on-demand service, extending evaluation from frontier model development to complex enterprise deployments and giving developers, buyers, auditors and boards a shared measurement language.
key_points: Candela launches with AILuminate Safety 1.2.1, covering twelve hazard categories from violent crime to specialized financial, health and legal advice, plus Jailbreak 1.1, which tests eleven categories with techniques such as typos, lookalike characters, 'ignore previous instructions,' context framing, deception and fragment assembly. Safety results for about 30 named open-weight models are public now, with jailbreak results to follow.

Results come in three tiers. Practice tests are inexpensive and free for MLCommons members, intended as frequent internal smoke tests. Annotated results expose every prompt-response-scored annotation tuple so teams can see which prompts drove a score and where to focus fixes. Official results use private prompts, are graded on a separate question set, and can be cited publicly in system cards, spec sheets or procurement decisions.

To keep scores credible, AILuminate keeps test prompts closed even from member companies and refreshes them as risks change. MLCommons runs scoring with a custom safety classifier rather than an LLM-as-a-judge, arguing it is more consistent and harder to fool on jailbreaks. Scores use item response theory, the statistics behind standardized tests, and report percentiles against a fixed reference panel.

Candela can test the system an organization actually runs, not just a base model. A local client relay lets teams evaluate models with their system prompt, retrieval, tools or agent loop. This matters because safety is not composable: a model that refuses a harmful request in release form may comply after fine-tuning, persona assignment, RAG-embedded instructions or tool inputs, while added guardrails can make a weaker model safer overall.

The platform is backed by MLCommons' broad membership and AIRR working groups, with more than 80 organizations deciding what to test and how to grade. Microsoft, NVIDIA and Google DeepMind endorsed the approach, citing enterprise evidence, published Nemotron scores and confidential enclave testing. MLCommons says future benchmarks will cover agentic security, privacy, psychosocial harms, industry-specific agent reliability and more languages and cultural contexts.
report.impact: Candela could push AI risk evaluation from ad hoc red teaming toward a shared, citable measurement layer. For the industry, it offers a vendor-neutral score that buyers, auditors and boards can compare, potentially simplifying procurement and governance. For developers, practice and annotated tests make safety checks cheaper and more diagnostic during development, while official results provide public evidence. For regular users, the payoff is safer deployed systems, but benchmarks are samples, not guarantees: closed prompts limit scrutiny, results depend on configuration, and access and pricing may shape who can use Candela. It also raises the stakes for independent oversight of MLCommons' methodology.
report.tools: Watch MLCommons Candela and AILuminate for official safety and jailbreak scores. For hands-on evaluation, try Inspect AI (UK AI Security Institute) for structured model evals, Stanford HELM for broad capability and risk benchmarking, NVIDIA Garak for LLM vulnerability scanning, and Promptfoo for prompt and red-team testing. These complement Candela's citable scoring by letting teams run local smoke tests, inspect failures and integrate checks into CI.
